column4: The section cites 44:13's question about remembrance after a clear messenger; this nearby ayah has the people ask for the punishment to be removed because they believe, a concrete plea made under the crisis.

After the plea in 44:12 and the messenger rejection in 44:14, this ayah says the punishment will be lifted briefly but they will return to their former course, showing how a reprieve can still be squandered.

The section cites 34:52's failed reach from a distant place; this immediately preceding ayah depicts the terrified people seized from a nearby place with no escape, sharpening the distance and lateness of their grasp.
The section connects 79:35's belated recollection to the great calamity; this next ayah says Hell is exposed for whoever sees, completing the Judgment scene that provokes the memory.

The section ties remembrance and the soul's life to 59:18; this next ayah warns against those who forgot God and were made to forget themselves, a specific opposite to the person's belated return to what their life meant.
The section follows the soul from its bodily life toward return and accounting; this ayah says the death one flees will meet them, then they will be returned to God and told what they did.

The section's person wishes too late that they had sent righteous work ahead; here the people in the Fire ask to be brought out to do good differently, and are reminded that they had time to remember and a warner came.

The section portrays a wish for more time after the final event; this warning says wrongdoers will ask their Lord for a short delay so they can respond and follow the messengers, a concrete version of that impossible postponement.
The section's human recognizes too late what should have been done; this ayah says that when the Hour comes suddenly, people lament what they neglected, matching the same sudden arrival and regret.
The section links the arrival of punishment with belated remembrance; this ayah says those who did wrong conceal regret when they see the punishment, tying the vision of the outcome to remorse.

The section's stated root ق د م describes good work as provision sent ahead; this ayah says whatever good people send ahead for themselves they will find with God, completing the forward-then-arrive relation.

The section's dictionary gloss for root ن ف س concerns the living soul, and it describes souls taken in sleep and death; this ayah says God takes people at night and raises them again by day, adding the recurring sleep-and-return scene.
The section contrasts its tranquil soul with a forced departure; this ayah depicts angels taking the disbelievers' souls while striking their faces and backs, another specific opposite death scene.

The section's tranquil soul is addressed and welcomed toward the Garden; here angels descend on those who remained steadfast and tell them not to fear or grieve, but to rejoice in the promised Garden.
The angelic welcome in 41:30 continues here with the promise of companionship in this life and the Hereafter and whatever the souls desire, extending the section's welcome to the returning soul.
This continuation calls the Garden a hospitality from the Forgiving and Merciful, specifying the welcome that follows the angelic reassurance in 41:30.
The section's late review of a person's life is staged in a Judgment sequence; this ayah says the records are opened before Hell is kindled and every soul knows what it brought.
The section's wish concerns what a person sent ahead for their life; this ayah says each person's record will be brought out on the Resurrection Day, making the life review an individual record.
After the record is brought out in 17:13, this ayah tells each person to read their book and serve as their own reckoner, a direct image of confronting what one has done.
The section says people mistake worldly ease for honor and realize the truth too late; this ayah describes a person who had been joyful among his family before the reckoning.
The family ease in 84:13 is followed by the person's belief that he would never return; this supplies the mistaken view of the afterlife that the section's late regret overturns.
This reply to the person who thought he would not return says his Lord had always seen him, completing the passage's correction of that false security.
